readerTitle: Pay for what people can actually move
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (가사 청소 회사, B2B IT 관리 서비스 회사) + 실제 연구 (Lazear 2000, Safelite 자동차 유리 설치) + 가상 적용 (소프트웨어 고객지원팀)
insight: 성과급의 비중은 의지의 문제가 아니라 설계의 문제다. 결과를 본인이 얼마나 움직일 수 있고, 얼마나 정확하고 빠르게 잴 수 있는지에 따라 고정급과 변동급의 비율을 정한다.
misconception: 성과에 따라 보상하면 누구에게나 동기부여가 된다. 성과급 비중이 클수록 좋은 보상 설계다.

sources.text: Lazear, E. P. (2000). Performance Pay and Productivity. American Economic Review, 90(5), 1346–1361.
청소 회사, IT 관리 서비스 회사, 소프트웨어 고객지원팀 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Safelite 연구: 시급제에서 개수당 지급(piece rate)으로 바꾼 뒤 1인당 생산량이 약 44% 늘었고, 그중 약 절반은 기존 직원의 생산성 증가, 나머지는 더 빠른 직원이 들어오고 남은 선별 효과라는 내용을 원문에서 다시 확인하세요.
Safelite가 개수당 지급과 함께 최저 시급 보장을 두었다는 점, 불량 설치는 해당 설치 기사에게 추적되어 무급으로 다시 작업하게 했다는 점을 Lazear(2000) 원문에서 확인하세요. 전환 시기는 1994~1995년경으로 알려져 있어 카드에는 'in the mid-1990s'로 적었습니다.
청소 회사의 시급 $20, IT 회사의 갱신 보너스 등은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 특정 국가의 노동법(최저임금, 성과급 관련 규정)은 다루지 않습니다.

cards.title: Pay for what people can actually move
body: Two owners make the same decision in the same month: *start paying for performance*.
One runs a house-cleaning company. Output goes up and the best cleaners earn more. The other runs an IT support firm for small offices. Within a year, two of her best account managers quit.
Same idea. Opposite results. The difference was in how the pay was designed.

image.label: Two storefronts, one cleaning van and one office, with pay slips
image.brief: 화면을 반으로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 청소 도구를 실은 밴과 웃는 청소 직원, 오른쪽은 노트북 앞에서 고개를 숙인 사무직 직원. 둘 다 같은 모양의 급여 명세서를 들고 있음. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your cleaners are slow.
body: You run a house-cleaning company. Cleaners earn $20 an hour and work alone. Jobs keep running past their estimates, and some cleaners are much faster than others with the same quality.
How do you change pay?

options.text: Raise everyone to $23 an hour to lift morale
options.feedback: It may help retention, but it costs more and still pays the slow and fast cleaner the same. Nothing about the work changes.

options.text: Pay a set rate per house, with a minimum hourly floor and spot checks on quality
options.feedback: Cleaners control their own speed and each house is easy to count. The floor limits their risk, and the checks stop speed from replacing quality.

options.text: Pay a set rate per house and let customers complain if quality drops
options.feedback: You reward speed and only notice corners being cut after a customer is already unhappy. Some never complain. They just leave.

cards.title: A bonus tied to something no one person controls.
body: The IT firm paid account managers a big bonus for every client that renewed its yearly contract.

But renewals depended on many things: how well technicians fixed problems, a server outage, a client being bought by a bigger company. One account manager did everything right and lost a third of her bonus when two clients merged.
The bonus felt like a lottery. The people with the best options elsewhere left first.

image.label: An account manager watching a renewal bar pushed by many hands
image.brief: 계약 갱신 게이지를 여러 손이 동시에 밀고 당기는 장면. 손에는 'Technicians', 'Outage', 'Client budget', 'Merger' 라벨. 계정 관리자는 옆에서 작은 손 하나만 얹고 있음.

cards.title: Matching the pay mix to the work
body: Most pay has two parts: a **fixed** part that arrives no matter what, and a **variable** part that moves with results. Designing pay is mostly choosing that mix and what the variable part is tied to.
Variable pay works when three things are true: the person largely controls the result, you can measure it fairly and soon, and the measure covers what you actually care about.
When those fail, pay mostly fixed and use other tools to guide effort.

image.label: A dial from fixed pay to variable pay with three checks
image.brief: 왼쪽 'Fixed', 오른쪽 'Variable'로 된 다이얼. 다이얼 아래 체크 3개: 'They control it', 'You can measure it', 'It covers what matters'. 체크가 많을수록 바늘이 오른쪽으로 감.

cards.title: When the conditions hold, the effect is large.
body: In the mid-1990s, Safelite, a US auto-glass company, moved its windshield installers from hourly pay to pay per windshield, with a guaranteed hourly minimum. Economist Edward Lazear studied the change.
Output per worker rose about **44%**. Roughly half came from existing installers working faster. The other half came from who stayed and who joined: faster installers were drawn to the new pay.
It fit the work. Installers controlled their pace, each job was countable, and faulty installs were traced back to the installer to fix.

cards.title: Run the three checks before you pick a number.
body: Put both businesses through the same questions.
list: **Do they control it?** Cleaner: mostly. Account manager: partly, alongside technicians and clients.
**Can you measure it fairly and soon?** Cleaner: every day. Account manager: once a year, with lots of luck mixed in.
**Does it cover what matters?** Cleaner: yes, if quality is checked. Account manager: renewals miss service and relationships.
cards.callout: The cleaner's job suits a large variable share. The account manager's suits a salary with a small shared bonus.
cards.softwareNote: The same test explains why software salespeople often have large commissions while engineers mostly get salary and equity. A closed deal is countable and owned by one rep. A shipped feature's value depends on many people and shows up slowly.

cards.title: Variable pay moves risk onto the worker.
body: When pay swings with results, a slow month hits the employee's rent, not just your margins. People with bills to pay value steady income, so a risky pay plan usually needs a floor or a higher expected total to attract good people.
There is a second cost. Whatever you pay for gets more attention, and whatever you leave out gets less. That is where incentives start to backfire, which is the next lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a software support team.
body: You run customer support for a software product. Agents handle tickets that range from a password reset to a bug that takes three teams to fix. The founder wants agents to "own" results with variable pay.
Which design fits?

options.text: A bonus for every ticket an agent closes
options.feedback: It's easy to count, but tickets differ hugely and hard ones need other teams. Agents learn to close fast and grab easy tickets, not to solve problems.

options.text: Mostly salary, plus a small team bonus based on reviewed quality and customer ratings each quarter
options.feedback: It matches the work: results are shared and only partly controlled, so the variable part is small, shared and checked. You give up some sharp incentive for fairness and focus.

options.text: Salary only, with no variable pay at all
options.feedback: Safe and fair, and often fine. But you miss a cheap way to point the whole team at quality and customer experience.

cards.title: Tie pay to results only as far as people can move them.
body: The more someone controls a result, and the better you can measure it, the more of their pay can depend on it. Otherwise, keep pay steady and guide effort in other ways.
**Try it today:** pick one role on your team. Ask the three questions: Do they control the result? Can I measure it fairly and soon? Does the measure cover what matters? Count the yes answers.
